sec.title: Background
sec.p: The combination of olaparib plus radium‐223 improved progression‐free survival in patients with metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer with bone metastases (BM) in the multicenter, randomized, phase 2 COMRADE trial (NCT03317391). Here, the patient‐reported outcome (PRO) analysis of this trial is reported.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Patients were randomized 1:1 to olaparib plus radium‐223 (arm A) or radium‐223 alone (arm B). PROs were assessed via the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Prostate (FACT‐P) and Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) at baseline and every 12 weeks. Clinically meaningful changes were defined as a ≥10‐point change in FACT‐P total score and a ≥30% or ≥2‐point change in BPI score. Mixed‐effects analysis‐of‐covariance models assessed PRO changes with adjustment for baseline characteristics among patients with baseline and ≥1 postbaseline assessment within 24 weeks.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of 114 treated patients, 74 (65%) were evaluable (arm A, n = 40; arm B, n = 34). Baseline characteristics were balanced, with a median age of 70–72 years and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 in 60%–62%, prior docetaxel in 50%–55%, >20 BM in 45%–47%, and pain medication use in 60%–72% of patients. No significant differences in FACT‐P total score change was observed at Week 12 (−4.87; 95% CI, −13.4 to 3.62) or Week 24 (1.79; 95% CI, −8.28 to 11.9). BPI pain severity did not differ at Week 12 (0.44; 95% CI, −0.44 to 1.33) or Week 24 (−0.20; 95% CI, −1.32 to 0.93). Arm B showed greater improvement in BPI pain interference at Week 12 (1.09; 95% CI, 0.14 to 2.05), which was not sustained at Week 24.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The addition of olaparib to radium‐223 was not associated with significant detriment to PROs or pain, which supports the tolerability of this combination.
Keywords: patient‐reported outcomes, poly(adenosine diphosphate ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, prostate cancer, quality of life, radiopharmaceuticals, radium‐223

abstract.title: Short abstract
abstract.p: In the randomized phase 2 COMRADE trial, addition of olaparib to radium‐223 did not significantly worsen quality‐of‐life or pain outcomes, with no clinically meaningful differences in Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Prostate or Brief Pain Inventory scores through 24 weeks in men with metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases. These findings support the tolerability of this combination, and provide important patient‐centered context for its clinical use.

sec.p: Revised 2026 May 10; Received 2026 Mar 21; Accepted 2026 May 12; Issue date 2026 Jul 1.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Bone metastases are the most common site of distant spread in men with metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), with occurrence in approximately 90% of patients with advanced disease. 1 The clinical burden of bone metastases is substantial, by contributing to significant morbidity, including skeletal‐related events such as pathologic fractures, spinal cord compression, and the need for palliative radiation or surgical intervention. 2 Beyond these discrete events, bone metastases are a major driver of chronic pain, functional decline, and impaired quality of life, which represent debilitating aspects of disease progression for patients living with mCRPC.

Radium‐223 is an α‐emitting radiopharmaceutical that selectively targets areas of increased bone turnover, and is approved for the treatment of mCRPC with symptomatic bone metastases. 3 In the pivotal phase 3 Alpha‐Emitter Radium‐223 and Survival in Patients With Symptomatic Bone Metastases in Castration‐Resistant Prostate Cancer (ALSYMPCA) trial, radium‐223 demonstrated a significant improvement in overall survival compared to placebo. Importantly, beyond survival benefits, radium‐223 was associated with meaningful improvements in patient‐reported outcomes (PROs), including delayed time to first opioid use, improved pain palliation, and better quality of life, as measured by the European Quality of Life 5‐Dimension and Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Prostate (FACT‐P) instruments. 4 , 5 These findings established radium‐223 not only as a life‐prolonging therapy but also as a treatment that addresses the symptomatic burden of bone metastases.

We conducted the Combination of Radium‐223 and Olaparib in Men With mCRPC and Bone Metastases (COMRADE) study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT03317391), a randomized phase 2 trial evaluating the addition of the poly(adenosine diphosphate ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor olaparib to radium‐223 in patients with mCRPC and bone metastases. 6 The rationale for this combination was based on preclinical evidence suggesting that PARP inhibition may enhance radiosensitivity by impairing DNA damage repair in tumor cells exposed to α‐particle radiation. The primary analysis demonstrated superior radiographic progression‐free survival (rPFS) with olaparib plus radium‐223 compared to radium‐223 alone, which supports the therapeutic potential of this combination strategy. 6

Pain control and preservation of quality of life are central treatment goals for patients with mCRPC and bone metastases. Understanding the impact of combination therapy on PROs is important for informing clinical decision‐making. Here, we report the PRO analysis from the COMRADE trial, which evaluated patient‐reported quality‐of‐life and pain outcomes with olaparib plus radium‐223 versus radium‐223 alone.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: The COMRADE study (NCT03317391) was a multicenter, randomized, open‐label, phase 2 trial conducted across academic centers in the United States via the National Cancer Institute Experimental Therapeutics Clinical Trials Network. The study design, eligibility criteria, and primary efficacy results have been previously reported. 6 Briefly, eligible patients had histologically or cytologically confirmed prostate cancer with progressive castration‐resistant disease per Prostate Cancer Working Group 3 criteria, ≥2 bone metastases by radiographic imaging, and no visceral metastases. 7 Prior therapy for mCRPC was permitted; however, patients could not have received previous treatment with PARP inhibitors or radium‐223. All patients received a bisphosphonate or denosumab unless medically contraindicated. An Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1 with adequate bone marrow and organ function was required. The institutional review board at each participating center approved the study, and all patients provided written informed consent.

Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive olaparib 200 mg orally twice daily continuously plus radium‐223 55 kBq/kg intravenously every 4 weeks for up to six cycles (arm A) or radium‐223 alone at the same dose and schedule (arm B). Randomization was stratified by prior docetaxel exposure (yes vs. no) and extent of bone disease (≤20 or >20 bone lesions). Patients in the radium‐223–alone arm were permitted to cross over to receive olaparib at the time of radiographic progression.

sec.title: PRO assessments
sec.p: PROs were assessed via the FACT‐P and Brief Pain Inventory Short Form (BPI‐SF), both of which are validated instruments commonly used in oncology clinical trials to evaluate quality of life and pain burden. 8 , 9 Questionnaires were administered at pretreatment Cycle 1 Day 1, every 12 weeks (±7 days), and at the end‐of‐study visit.

The FACT‐P is a validated, self‐administered questionnaire that consists of the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–General, which includes 27 items across four well‐being domains (physical well‐being, social/family well‐being, emotional well‐being, and functional well‐being), and the Prostate Cancer Subscale, which includes 12 prostate cancer–specific items addressing symptoms such as pain, urinary function, and sexual function. 8 The FACT‐P total score is the sum of all 39 items and ranges from 0 to 156, with higher scores indicating better quality of life. A domain score was calculated if more than 50% of items in that domain were completed; if any domain score was missing, the total score was not calculated.

The BPI‐SF is a widely used, validated instrument for assessing cancer‐related pain. 9 It includes four pain severity items (worst pain, least pain, average pain, and current pain in the last 24 h) and seven pain interference items (general activity, mood, walking ability, normal work, relations with other people, sleep, and enjoyment of life) each rated on 0–10 numerical rating scales, with higher scores indicating worse pain. Pain severity was scored as the mean of the four pain items if at least two of the four items were completed. Pain interference was scored as the mean of the seven interference items if at least four of the seven items were completed.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The PRO analysis was conducted in the as‐treated population, and was limited to patients with a baseline assessment and at least one postbaseline assessment at Weeks 12 and/or 24. Given the low questionnaire completion rates beyond 24 weeks, the primary analyses focused on PRO changes during the first 24 weeks after treatment initiation. All hypothesis‐testing analyses were post hoc. Descriptive analyses for all follow‐up assessments up to 48 weeks are provided in the supplement. For patients in arm B who crossed over to receive olaparib, both PRO data and the expected follow‐up were truncated at the date of crossover.

Clinically meaningful changes were defined via established minimal clinically important differences. For the FACT‐P total score, meaningful improvement was defined as an increase of ≥10 points from baseline, and meaningful worsening was defined as a decrease of ≥10 points from baseline. For BPI pain severity and pain interference, worsening was defined as an increase of at least 30% or at least 2 points from baseline. The percentages of patients experiencing clinically meaningful changes were summarized at Weeks 12 and 24 and for the combined 12‐ and 24‐week assessment period.

Mixed‐effects analysis‐of‐covariance (ANCOVA) regression models were used to assess the average treatment effect on changes in PRO scores from baseline. The dependent variable was the change from baseline at Weeks 12 and 24. Covariates included treatment arm, baseline PRO score, time point, age, and ECOG performance status. Least‐squares (LS) mean changes were reported at each time point for each treatment arm, along with between‐arm differences and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All analyses were performed with SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc, Cary, North Carolina).

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: Of 120 patients randomized in the COMRADE trial, 114 received allocated treatment (arm A, n = 59; arm B, n = 55). Of these, 74 patients (65%) were included in the PRO‐evaluable population (arm A, n = 40; arm B, n = 34) (Figure S1). Forty patients were not evaluable because of missing baseline and/or postbaseline assessments within the 24‐week analysis window. Of the evaluable patients, 71 (62%) were evaluable for FACT‐P total score and 72 (63%) for BPI pain severity and pain interference.

Baseline characteristics were well balanced between arms (Table 1). Median age was 70 years (interquartile range [IQR], 62–77 years) in arm A and 72 years (IQR, 66–76 years) in arm B, with an ECOG performance status of 1 in 60% and 62% of patients, respectively. Prior docetaxel had been received by 55% versus 50% of patients in the combination versus radium‐223–alone arms. Extent of bone disease was similar, with >20 bone metastases present in 45% versus 47% of patients. Baseline pain medication use was numerically higher in the radium‐223–alone arm (any pain medication, 72% vs. 60%; opioid medication, 50% vs. 33%). When compared to the overall intent‐to‐treat population, baseline characteristics in the PRO‐evaluable population were also similar. 6

sec.title: FACT‐P analysis
sec.p: Questionnaire completion rates for the FACT‐P were 76% and 80% at baseline, 66% and 71% at Week 12, and 44% and 56% at Week 24 in arms A and B, respectively, with rates declining beyond 24 weeks (Table S1). Baseline FACT‐P total scores were similar between arms (mean, 106.7 [standard deviation (SD), 21.6] vs. 109.4 [SD, 23.0]), as were scores across the individual domains, including physical well‐being, social/family well‐being, emotional well‐being, and functional well‐being, and the Prostate Cancer Subscale (Table S2).

In the primary adjusted analysis, there were no significant differences in LS mean change from baseline in FACT‐P total scores between arms at Week 12 (arm A, −5.09 [standard error (SE), 2.77] vs. arm B, −0.23 [SE, 3.17]; difference, −4.87; 95% CI, −13.4 to 3.62) or Week 24 (arm A, −1.41 [SE, 3.28] vs. arm B, −3.20 [SE, 3.73]; difference, 1.79; 95% CI, −8.28 to 11.9) (Table 2).

sec.p: Exploratory descriptive analyses were broadly consistent with the adjusted findings. Unadjusted FACT‐P total scores remained stable over time in both arms, with no sustained separation between treatment groups (Figure 1A; Table S2). At the domain level, subscale scores were similar between arms across time points (Figure 1B–F), although mean Prostate Cancer Subscale scores showed a modest numerical decline at Week 12 in the combination arm (27.5 vs. 29.9) that was not sustained at Week 24 (30.6 vs. 29.4). Rates of clinically meaningful FACT‐P worsening by 24 weeks were similar between the combination and radium‐223–alone arms (40% vs. 42%), as were rates of improvement (23% vs. 32%), although these analyses were limited by small sample sizes at later time points (Table S3).

sec.title: BPI analysis
sec.p: Questionnaire completion rates for the BPI‐SF were 76% and 78% at baseline, 66% and 71% at Week 12, and 44% and 56% at Week 24 in arms A and B, respectively, with rates declining beyond 24 weeks (Table S4). Baseline mean BPI‐SF pain severity scores were similar between arms (3.1 [SD, 2.3] vs. 2.9 [SD, 2.2]), as were baseline mean BPI pain interference scores (3.3 [SD, 2.5] vs. 2.8 [SD, 2.5]) (Tables S5 and S6).

In the adjusted analysis, there were no significant differences in LS mean change from baseline in BPI‐SF pain severity between arms at Week 12 (arm A, 0.11 [SE, 0.30] vs. arm B, −0.33 [SE, 0.32]; difference, 0.44; 95% CI, −0.44 to 1.33) or Week 24 (arm A, 0.24 [SE, 0.37] vs. arm B, 0.44 [SE, 0.42]; difference, −0.20; 95% CI, −1.32 to 0.93) (Table 2). For BPI pain interference, arm B showed a significantly greater decrease at Week 12 (arm A, 0.21 [SE, 0.32] vs. arm B, −0.88 [SE, 0.35]; difference, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.14 to 2.05); however, this difference was not sustained at Week 24 (arm A, −0.47 [SE, 0.36] vs. arm B, −0.20 [SE, 0.41]; difference, −0.27; 95% CI, −1.37 to 0.82) (Table 2).

Exploratory descriptive analyses were consistent with the adjusted findings. Rates of clinically meaningful worsening in pain severity by 24 weeks were similar between the combination and radium‐223–alone arms (31% vs. 30%), as were rates of worsening in pain interference (33% vs. 34%) (Table S7). Unadjusted BPI‐SF pain severity and pain interference scores remained generally stable over time in both arms (Figure 1G,H; Tables S5 and S6).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: In this PRO analysis of the randomized phase 2 COMRADE trial, the addition of olaparib to radium‐223 was not associated with significant detriment to patient‐reported quality of life or pain compared to radium‐223 alone in patients with mCRPC and bone metastases. Across all measures evaluated, including FACT‐P total score and individual subscale domains, BPI pain severity, and BPI‐SF pain interference, no sustained or clinically meaningful differences were observed between treatment arms through 24 weeks. Both adjusted and unadjusted analyses yielded concordant findings, and rates of clinically meaningful worsening were similar between arms across instruments. Importantly, findings were concordant across disease‐specific quality‐of‐life (FACT‐P) and pain‐specific (BPI‐SF) measures, which reinforces the consistency and reliability of the overall PRO findings. Taken together, these data support the tolerability of the olaparib plus radium‐223 combination from the patient perspective.

Pain control and preservation of quality of life are central therapeutic goals for patients with mCRPC and bone metastases, a population in which skeletal morbidity substantially contributes to functional decline, chronic pain, and impaired well‐being. In the pivotal ALSYMPCA trial, radium‐223 not only improved overall survival but was also associated with significant quality‐of‐life benefits, including a higher proportion of patients experiencing meaningful FACT‐P improvement (25% vs. 16%; p = .020) and delayed quality‐of‐life deterioration compared to placebo. 3 , 4 Notably, ALSYMPCA required symptomatic bone disease, defined as regular analgesic medication use for cancer‐related bone pain or treatment with external beam radiation therapy within the preceding 12 weeks, which ensured a population with substantial baseline pain burden and a dynamic range for detecting improvement. More recently, the phase 3 PEACE‐3 trial demonstrated that the addition of radium‐223 to enzalutamide significantly improved rPFS and overall survival in first‐line mCRPC; however, PEACE‐3 enrolled asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic patients, and quality‐of‐life data from that study have not yet been reported. 10 Our findings extend this evolving landscape by providing the first PRO data evaluating a PARP inhibitor combined with a radiopharmaceutical, and demonstrate that the addition of olaparib to radium‐223 does not negatively affect the PROs associated with backbone radiopharmaceutical therapy, despite the potential for additive toxicity with combination treatment.

In the adjusted ANCOVA, FACT‐P total score changes from baseline were not significantly different between arms at either Week 12 or 24. Although the combination arm showed a numerically greater decline at Week 12 (LS mean change, −5.09 vs. −0.23), this difference did not reach statistical significance and was not sustained at Week 24, at which point both arms showed comparable declines. The magnitude of the Week 12 difference (−4.87 points) was below the established minimal clinically important difference of 10 points for the FACT‐P total score, which further supports its limited clinical relevance. At the domain level, unadjusted subscale scores were generally stable across time points, with a modest numerical decline in the Prostate Cancer Subscale at Week 12 in the combination arm that resolved by Week 24, which potentially reflects early treatment‐related symptom burden that attenuated with continued therapy.

The BPI analysis similarly demonstrated no significant between‐arm differences in pain severity at either time point. Baseline pain scores were relatively low in both arms (mean BPI pain severity, approximately 3 on a 0–10 scale), consistent with the eligibility criteria for COMRADE, which, unlike ALSYMPCA, did not require symptomatic bone disease. 3 This lower baseline symptom burden is more comparable to the asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic population enrolled in PEACE‐3, and limits the dynamic range for detecting treatment‐related improvements in pain. 10 This floor effect represents an important consideration when interpreting the absence of differential treatment effects on pain severity. The greater decrease in BPI pain interference in the radium‐223–alone arm at Week 12 (difference, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.14 to 2.05) should be interpreted cautiously. The difference was modest, not sustained at Week 24, and not corroborated by parallel findings in BPI pain severity or any FACT‐P domain. Baseline imbalances may also have contributed, given that patients in the radium‐223–alone arm had numerically higher baseline pain medication use, opioid use, and osteoclast‐targeted therapy, which provides greater room for improvement.

The absence of meaningful PRO deterioration is reassuring, given the longer treatment exposure and higher rate of grade ≥3 adverse events in the combination arm (56% vs. 33%), primarily hematologic, including lymphopenia (31% vs. 9.1%), anemia (22% vs. 16%), and thrombocytopenia (6.8% vs. 3.6%). Because many of these events were laboratory based, they may not always translate into patient‐perceived symptoms, consistent with the preserved quality‐of‐life and pain outcomes observed.

Our findings are consistent with the broader body of evidence on PARP inhibitor effects on PROs in mCRPC. 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 In the phase 3 PROfound trial, olaparib monotherapy was associated with reduced pain burden and better preserved quality of life compared to physician's choice of next‐generation hormonal therapy in patients with homologous recombination repair gene alterations. 11 , 14 Similarly, in a phase 2 trial of olaparib plus abiraterone versus placebo plus abiraterone, no significant differences in quality of life or pain were observed between arms, which suggests that the addition of olaparib to a standard backbone therapy does not meaningfully compromise PROs. 12 A recent systematic review and meta‐analysis of PARP inhibitor trials in mCRPC further corroborated these findings by reporting no clinically meaningful deterioration in quality of life with PARP inhibitor treatment. 13 The phase 1 LuPARP trial is similarly evaluating the combination of a PARP inhibitor with a radiopharmaceutical (177Lu‐PSMA‐617 plus olaparib) and has demonstrated promising efficacy and tolerability, although PRO data from that study have not yet been reported. 15 The COMRADE PRO data add to this evidence by extending these observations to a radiopharmaceutical combination context not previously evaluated for PRO impact.

This study has several limitations. The PRO analysis was exploratory, and the study was not powered for PRO comparisons. No adjustment for multiplicity was applied, and the modest sample size yields wide CIs around between‐arm differences and limits the ability to detect small but potentially clinically relevant effects. These findings should therefore be considered hypothesis generating. Beyond data truncation at the time of crossover, a notable proportion of treated patients were not PRO evaluable, and completion rates declined over time. Given that reasons for noncompletion were not systematically captured, the potential for informative missingness cannot be fully excluded. Declining questionnaire completion over time, coupled with the rPFS benefit favoring the combination arm, may also have resulted in differential attrition between arms. Patients evaluable at later time points in both arms were enriched for those with sustained disease control, and the degree of this enrichment may have differed between arms, which could potentially obscure true between‐arm differences. Additional limitations include the open‐label design, which may have introduced expectation bias in patient‐reported responses, and the crossover design, which necessitated truncation of PRO data at the crossover date and may have underestimated longer term differences between arms. Despite these limitations, the use of validated instruments, adjusted statistical models, and concordance across multiple PRO end points strengthens the interpretability of the findings.

In conclusion, the addition of olaparib to radium‐223 in the COMRADE trial was not associated with significant detriment to patient‐reported quality of life or pain burden compared to radium‐223 alone. These PRO findings, together with the previously reported rPFS benefit, support the tolerability and clinical viability of this combination strategy in patients with mCRPC and bone metastases. As radiopharmaceutical combination strategies continue to evolve, including the PEACE‐3 regimen of radium‐223 plus enzalutamide and emerging radiopharmaceutical–PARP inhibitor approaches, prospective and adequately powered PRO assessments will be essential to fully characterize the patient experience with these novel treatment combinations.
